With everything settled so agreeably and satisfactorily, the agreement was solemnly confirmed over another teacup of the peppermint mixture, made all the more necessary by the lady's nervous excitement. While they drank it, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very well,” said the gentleman, sipping his peppermint. “I'll stop at Sowerberry's on my way home and tell him to send someone tomorrow morning. Was that what frightened you, love?”

“It wasn't anything in particular, dear,” the lady said evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble insisted. “Won't you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” the lady replied. “One of these days. After we're married, dear.”

“After we're married!” exclaimed Mr. Bumble. “It wasn't some insolence from one of those male paupers that—”

“No, no, love!” the lady quickly interrupted.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble continued, “if I thought any one of them had dared to raise his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn't have dared, love,” the lady answered.

“They'd better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. “Just let me see any man, from this parish or anywhere else, who would presume to do it, and I can tell him he wouldn't do it twice!”

Without the accompaniment of his violent gestures, this might not have sounded like a particularly flattering tribute to the lady's beauty. But Mr. Bumble delivered his threat with so many warlike movements that she was deeply touched by this evidence of devotion, and declared with great admiration that he truly was a dove.

The dove then turned up his coat collar and put on his cocked hat. After exchanging a long, affectionate embrace with his future wife, he ventured once more into the cold night wind. He stopped only for a few minutes in the male paupers' ward to berate them a little, reassuring himself that he could perform the duties of workhouse master with the necessary harshness. Satisfied with his qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building lighthearted, his mind full of glowing prospects of promotion that occupied him until he reached the undertaker's shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper; and Noah Claypole was never inclined to make any greater physical effort than he needed to eat and drink comfortably. Consequently, the shop remained open, although the usual closing time had passed. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane against the counter several times without attracting anyone's attention. Then, seeing a light through the glass window of the little sitting room behind the shop, he ventured to look inside and discover what was happening. What he discovered surprised him considerably.

It was after two when a sudden turn brought me close to the lake, near a cove where a little rowing boat lay moored. Our house was not far away, and I could see my father and aunt walking on the lawn. I jumped into the boat and, being thoroughly accustomed to such adventures, pushed off from the shore and put all my strength into rowing swiftly across. My father has often told me that, approaching in my white dress with only my tartan rachan wrapped around me, my hair streaming over my shoulders and the boat flying faster than anyone could have thought I could propel it, I looked more like a spirit than a human girl. As I reached the shore, my father steadied the boat; I sprang lightly out and a moment later was in his arms.

Now my life truly began. Everything around me changed from a dull sameness into a brilliant scene of joy and delight. The happiness of being with my father went far beyond even my most hopeful expectations. We were constantly together, and never ran out of things to discuss. He had spent his sixteen years away among peoples almost unknown in Europe. He had traveled through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, entering the homes of the inhabitants with a freedom granted to few Europeans. His accounts of their customs, his stories, and his descriptions of the countryside filled delightful hours whenever we grew tired of discussing our own plans for the future.

Affection was so unfamiliar to me that I listened in delight to every word when he described his feelings for me during those long years of seeming neglect. “At first,” he said, “I could not bear to think of my poor little girl. But later, as my grief diminished and hope returned, you were the one person my thoughts could turn to. Among cities and deserts, your little fairy figure, as I imagined it, was always drifting before my eyes. The northern breeze felt sweeter and gentler as it refreshed me, because it seemed to bring something of your spirit with it. I often thought of returning at once and taking you away with me to some fertile island where we could live in peace forever. On my journey home, so many fears broke in upon my passionate hopes that my impatience became almost unbearable. I did not dare imagine that the sun might shine and the moon rise over your grave instead of your living form. But no, that has not happened. I have my Mathilda, my comfort and my hope.”

She and the children could easily stay.”

“Ah, Papa, you have never managed to arrange that, and I don't believe you ever will. Isabella cannot bear to stay anywhere without her husband.”

This was too plainly true to argue with. Much as Mr. Woodhouse disliked it, he could only sigh in resignation. Emma saw that the thought of his daughter's devotion to her husband had lowered his spirits, so she immediately turned the conversation toward something that would cheer him up.

“Harriet must spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I am sure she will enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, aren't we, Papa? I wonder who she will think is better looking, Henry or John?”

“Yes, I wonder which. Poor little darlings, how pleased they will be to come. They love visiting Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I'm sure they do, sir. I certainly don't know anyone who doesn't.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John looks very much like his mother. Henry is the oldest; he was named after me, rather than his father. John, the second boy, was named after his father. I believe some people are surprised that the eldest wasn't, but Isabella insisted on calling him Henry, which I thought very sweet of her. And he really is a very clever boy. They are all remarkably clever and have so many charming little habits. They come and stand beside my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, could you give me a piece of string?’ Once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives were made only for grandpapas. I often think their father treats them too roughly.”

“He seems rough to you,” Emma said, “because you are so gentle yourself. But if you could compare him with other fathers, you wouldn't think so. He wants his boys to be active and strong, and he sometimes speaks sharply to them when they misbehave. But he is a loving father—Mr. John Knightley certainly is a loving father. All the children are fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and throws them up toward the ceiling in the most frightening way!”

“But they love it, Papa. Nothing makes them happier. They enjoy it so much that if their uncle didn't insist they take turns, whichever child went first would never let the next one have a go.”

“Well, I cannot understand it.”

“We are all like that, Papa. Half the world cannot understand what the other half enjoys.”
